clue.text: Rejected informal agreement to confine boy when hormones rage

indicators.note: to confine something is to hold it within, so the boy's name goes inside
something rejected is turned back, so the word for the agreement is read backwards

parts.note: yup is a casual way of saying yes
Bert is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A spurned casual deal and a lad kept in, at the age when teenagers are hormonal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejected' signals the reversal of the casual yes, and 'to confine' says the boy's name sits inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Adolescence, the stage of sexual maturing, is the time of life marked by raging hormones.

clue.text: Expert urbanely concealing disquiet

indicators.note: the two words conceal a run of letters spanning their join

explanation.surface: A smooth expert hides his unease.
explanation.definitionFit: To disquiet someone is to unsettle or worry them, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Pompous BBC aims to change

indicators.note: to change the letters of the three words is to put them in a new order

explanation.surface: The BBC sets out to alter its overblown style.
explanation.definitionFit: Bombast is inflated, pretentious language, so a pompous speaker is described with this adjective.

clue.text: Poem of Frost read aloud

indicators.note: the synonym for frost, spoken, gives a word of the same sound

parts.note: rime is hoar frost

explanation.surface: A poem by Robert Frost being recited.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to the poet Robert Frost, but here frost is RIME, ice crystals.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhyme can mean a short verse or poem, as in a nursery rhyme.

clue.text: Fancy any old guy or girl

indicators.note: fancy as an adjective means elaborate or ornamented, so the letters are dressed up in a new order

explanation.surface: Would any old bloke or lass take your fancy?
explanation.definitionFit: A girl, especially a well-mannered one, is politely called this phrase.

clue.text: Taking most unfavourable view of opener, conclusively stumped on a pair

indicators.note: in an across answer one piece on another follows it, so the cricket letters come after the pair

parts.note: a pair is a two, written A TWO

indicators.note: conclusively points to the final letter of the word opener

parts.note: ST is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for stumped

explanation.surface: A cricket commentary: the opening batsman stumped having scored only two, a gloomy assessment.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an opener is a batsman who goes in first, and being stumped is a way of getting out.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means if the worst happens, so it describes taking the most pessimistic outlook.

clue.text: Extremely alcoholic free bitter!

indicators.note: the extreme letters of alcoholic, its first and last

parts.note: to rid is to free, clear of something

explanation.surface: An exclamation praising strong, alcohol-free bitter beer.
explanation.walkthrough: Bitter here is not British beer (a hoppy ale) but the adjective for a sharp taste.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrid describes a sharp, pungent, harsh taste or smell, close to bitter.

clue.text: Capricious male thus pursuing wife, a student

indicators.note: pursuing means following, so the man and thus come after the wife

parts.note: him refers to a male
sic is Latin for thus
L is a learner driver, a student

explanation.surface: A fickle man chasing a wife and a student as well.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone capricious acts on sudden whims, so is fanciful and unpredictable.

clue.text: Demolishes Freudianism on a regular basis

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals, here the second, fourth and so on

explanation.surface: Someone tears apart Freud's theories routinely.
explanation.definitionFit: To ruin a thing is to destroy it, so the verb matches demolishes.

clue.text: It causes butterflies in nets to flap, taking in oxygen

indicators.note: the jumbled letters take another letter inside them
flapping shakes things about, so the letters of in and nets are jumbled

parts.note: O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A lepidopterist's scene of butterflies fluttering in nets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to flap' rearranges INNETS into TENSIN, and 'taking in' puts O inside it. Butterflies here are nervous flutters in the stomach.
explanation.definitionFit: Nervous strain or anxiety produces the fluttery feeling people call butterflies in the stomach.

clue.text: Clubs withdrawing from rubbish game

indicators.note: the letter for clubs pulls out of the word for rubbish

parts.note: crummy means rubbish, poor quality
C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs

explanation.surface: A card player gives up clubs from a poor hand in a game.
explanation.definitionFit: Rummy is a card game in which players collect sets and sequences.

clue.text: British weather starts to irritate absurdly nervy Slav

parts.note: UK, the United Kingdom, stands for British
rain is a kind of weather

indicators.note: the starts of the three words, their first letters

explanation.surface: A jittery Slav finds British weather maddening.
explanation.definitionFit: Ukrainians are an East Slavic people, so one is an example of a Slav.

clue.text: Arousal of nude vegan not requited

indicators.note: arousal stirs things up, so the letters are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A naked vegan's excitement is not returned.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests unreturned love, but requited here means avenged, a wrong repaid.
explanation.definitionFit: To requite a wrong is to repay it, so a wrong not requited has had no revenge.

clue.text: Ultimately amateurs, you useless English samurai make Japanese scoff

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so the last letter of each word is taken

explanation.surface: Inept amateurs and a hopeless English samurai prepare a Japanese meal.
explanation.walkthrough: Scoff is British slang for food.
explanation.definitionFit: Sushi is a Japanese dish of vinegared rice with raw fish, so it is Japanese food.

clue.text: Brit errs, relinquishing rights for morsels of food

indicators.note: to relinquish is to give up, so these letters are removed from the words before

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right, so rights here are three R letters

explanation.surface: A Briton makes mistakes and gives up rights in exchange for food.
explanation.walkthrough: BRITERRS holds three Rs; take all three away to leave the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Bites are small mouthfuls, so they are little pieces of something to eat.

clue.text: Refuse to eat tiny tot's last vegetable

indicators.note: eating takes something inside, so the other pieces go into the word for refuse

parts.note: to scorn something is to refuse or reject it with contempt
wee is Scottish for tiny

indicators.note: last picks the final letter of tot

explanation.surface: A toddler refuses to eat the last of the vegetables.
explanation.definitionFit: Maize kernels eaten as food are a common vegetable, yellow and sweet.

clue.text: Dependence Day, in a manner of speaking

indicators.note: the letter for day goes in among the following words

parts.note: diction is one's manner of speaking

explanation.surface: Independence Day, or so to speak, a play on the American holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue plays on Independence Day: with the 'In' detached, Dependence is left as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Dependence on a drug or habit is a craving or compulsion that cannot be given up easily.

clue.text: Houses large number comfortably in empty garages

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral 500, a large number
well means comfortably, as in well off

indicators.note: empty leaves only the outside letters of garages

explanation.surface: Many cars fit snugly into vacant garages.
explanation.definitionFit: Dwellings are homes or residences, places where people live.

clue.text: Reckless rogue with dirty books

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous rascal or rogue
rude means dirty, smutty
NT, the New Testament, is a set of books

explanation.surface: A careless scoundrel with smutty literature.
explanation.definitionFit: Imprudent means unwise and heedless of consequences, the same as rash.

clue.text: Typical example of drug ingested by Norman?

indicators.note: ingested means swallowed, so the drug goes inside the other word

parts.note: a Norman arch is one arch type in architecture
E is short for ecstasy, the drug

explanation.surface: A drug swallowed by a man named Norman.
explanation.walkthrough: Norman looks like a man's name, but it is a style of arch, so it defines ARCH TYPE.
explanation.definitionFit: An archetype is a perfect model or classic instance of a kind.

clue.text: As one, enthralled by cranes flying

indicators.note: held captive by, so the numeral sits inside the other letters
flying birds move about, so the letters of cranes are mixed up

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: As one, watchers are captivated by cranes in flight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flying' rearranges CRANES into ARSENC, and 'enthralled by' puts I inside. As is a chemical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: As is the chemical symbol for the poisonous element number 33.

clue.text: Eagerly welcome LaMotta, discontented young boxer?

indicators.note: without content, so only the outside letters of LaMotta remain

parts.note: a boxer is a dog breed, and a young dog is a pup

explanation.surface: Jake LaMotta, the boxer, unhappy with a new young fighter.
explanation.walkthrough: Jake LaMotta was a real boxer, which makes 'boxer' read as a fighter, not the dog breed.
explanation.definitionFit: To receive something enthusiastically is to lap it up, like a dog drinking.

clue.text: Kitty's on barricade in German city

indicators.note: in a down answer the first piece sits on top of the second

parts.note: a kitty is a pot of money, so with the apostrophe s it gives pot's
a dam is a barrier across water

explanation.surface: A cat perched on a barricade in a German city.
explanation.definitionFit: Potsdam is a city near Berlin, capital of the state of Brandenburg.

clue.text: Rent place on Adriatic

definitions.meaning: rent as a noun is a tear, as a verb past tense, torn
a Croatian city on the Adriatic coast

explanation.surface: Renting a place on the Adriatic coast.
explanation.definitionFit: A tear is a crack or division; the Croatian port city has this name too.

clue.text: Set about turning 60 in a relaxed way

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for set goes around the numeral

parts.note: to lay is to set down

indicators.note: turning means the Roman numeral is read backwards

parts.note: LX is 60 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Someone about to turn sixty takes it easy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' reverses the Roman sixty, and 'about' wraps the word for set around the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Laxly means loosely, without strictness, so it fits casually or slackly.

clue.text: Try to jump over bar in eastern European wine cellar

parts.note: a Pole comes from Poland in eastern Europe
a vault is an underground cellar for wine

explanation.surface: Attempting to leap the bar in a Polish wine cellar.
explanation.definitionFit: The athletics event has a vaulter use a long pole to clear a high horizontal bar.

clue.text: People on vacation knocking back fine English tea

indicators.note: vacated, so the inside is empty and only the outer letters of people stay
knocking back means the word for fine is turned backwards

parts.note: OK means fine

explanation.surface: Holidaymakers downing a fine English cup of tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Pekoe is a grade of black tea made from young leaves.

clue.text: Rancour in van, missing an M1 turning

indicators.note: missing means lacking, so the letters of an go from van
turning means the spelled-out M1 is read backwards

parts.note: M1 is M plus ONE, written out

explanation.surface: Road rage in a van after missing the M1 turning.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is Britain's main motorway from London to Leeds. Spelt M ONE, 'turning' reverses it to ENOM.
explanation.definitionFit: Venom figuratively means spite, bitter hostility, the same as rancour.

clue.text: Closest relation of wild fox in Kent

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: The nearest relative of a wild fox living in Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent is a county in south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: One's nearest family member, in legal terms, is named as this phrase.

clue.text: Large amount of revolting gas inside of Ada

indicators.note: revolting means turning over, so the gas's name is read backwards

parts.note: neon is a noble gas

indicators.note: the inside of Ada is its middle letter

explanation.surface: A lot of foul gas inside someone named Ada.
explanation.definitionFit: As in no end of trouble, the phrase means a great deal or very many.

clue.text: Spice from island in French north-east

parts.note: a cay is a small low island
en is French for in

explanation.surface: A spice that comes from an island in north-eastern France.
explanation.definitionFit: This hot red pepper powder is a culinary seasoning from dried chillies.

clue.text: Lousy MP to mask overwhelming evidence of something wrong

indicators.note: the words overwhelm, that is cover over, a run of letters running across them

explanation.surface: A shabby politician covering up overwhelming proof of wrongdoing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overwhelming' looks like part of the evidence phrase but it is the signal that the answer is held in the words before.
explanation.definitionFit: A sign or indication of illness or of a problem is called by this word.
